profile_summary: This respondent may see men and women as shaped by different social roles and interests in everyday life, parenting, and workplace strengths, while also believing that basic physical capacity and emotional expression overlap substantially across individuals.

This respondent sees many everyday differences as shaped by social norms and interests rather than by broad capability. They think men and women often gravitate toward different hobbies and may develop different workplace strengths, but view physical capacity, parenting, and emotional expression as more overlapping than distinct.

This respondent sees men and women as sharing many individual interests and workplace talents, while still believing that embodied differences and socialized roles often lead to different physical capabilities, parenting styles, and ways of expressing emotions.

This respondent sees men and women as often drawn to different interests and styles of emotional expression, and also perceives some gendered patterns in workplace strengths. At the same time, they think men and women are broadly alike in core physical capacity and in how they approach caring for children.

This respondent sees gendered social expectations as still influencing hobbies and parenting styles, but thinks men and women largely overlap in physical capability, emotional expression, and workplace strengths.

This respondent sees many gender differences as emerging from social roles, expectations, and experience rather than from broad limits in capacity. They think men and women often gravitate toward different interests, parenting habits, and workplace strengths, while still believing they are generally similar in physical potential and in their capacity to express emotions.

This respondent tends to see everyday preferences and caregiving or emotional styles as shaped more by individual personality and social experience than by gender, while still believing that average physical differences and some workplace strengths can lead men and women to be better suited to different tasks.

This respondent tends to see most observed gender differences as shaped more by individual personality, opportunity, and social expectations than by fundamental differences between men and women, while still allowing that some differences may appear in particular situations.
